clinical_record:
A man in his 60s presented with a 1-year history of a pruritic, dark red plaque on his right upper eyelid. No remarkable medical history was noted.

A 4 × 2-cm erythematous, violaceous, indurated, scaly plaque with some papules on his right upper eyelid.

- Laboratory Tests: Routine blood tests and biochemistry analysis were within normal limits.- Histopathologic Examination:  - Revealed perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrates around cystically dilated follicular infundibula  - Exocytosis of atypical lymphocytes into the epithelium  - Admixed plasma cells, eosinophils, and multinucleate giant cells  - Alcian blue staining showed focal mild follicular mucin deposition- Immunohistochemical Analysis:  - Lymphocytic infiltrates positive for CD3, CD4, CD5, and CD7  - Negative for CD8, CD20, CD30, CD79a, and CD56  - CD4 to CD8 cells ratio within hair follicles > 7:1  - Monoclonal T-cell gene rearrangement was demonstrated- Images:  Image A Title: Clinical presentation of right upper eyelid  Image A Description: 4 × 2-cm erythematous, violaceous, indurated, scaly plaque with papules    Image B Title: Lesional specimen  Image B Description: Histopathologic examination at original magnification ×50    Image C Title: High-power magnification of histopathologic examination  Image C Description: Shows atypical lymphocytes    Image D Title: Immunohistochemical staining  Image D Description: Shows lymphocytic infiltrates predominantly positive for CD4

What is the most likely diagnosis?

candidate_registry.label: Primary cutaneous CD4+ small/medium T-cell lymphoma

clinical_record:
A primigravid patient in their 20s during the eighth month of gestation presented with history of regular nonexertional episodic palpitations that lasted for a few minutes and subsided spontaneously over the past several days. The patient had no associated sweating, syncope, dyspnoea, orthopnoea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Visible neck pulsation was noticed by the patient's mother. The patient had no chronic medical comorbid conditions and was not taking any medications.

Blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg and heart rate was 120 beats/min. The general examination was unremarkable. The jugular venous pulsations revealed regular cannon waves, and auscultation was significant for a variable first heart sound. Examination findings of other systems were normal.

- Laboratory tests: Complete blood cell count, kidney function, liver function, thyroid function, serum electrolytes, and cardiac troponin were within normal limits.- Imaging/Other tests:   - 2-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography showed good biventricular function and normally functioning valves    - ECG findings:    Image Title: ECG taken at admission    Image Description: Regular narrow QRS tachycardia (QRS duration, 60 milliseconds) at a ventricular rate of 103-125 beats/min with mean cycle length of 509.16 milliseconds, QRS axis of +60°, and QTc of 404 milliseconds. Regular P waves evident marching onto QRS complexes at a rate of 100-125 beats/min with mean cycle length of 517.16 milliseconds with varying PR intervals.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Accelerated atrioventricular junctional tachycardia with isorhythmic atrioventricular dissociation

candidate_registry.label: Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia due to Atrioventricular Nodal Reentrant Tachycardia

clinical_record:
A woman in her 80s presented to the emergency department with altered mental status, weakness, slurred speech, emesis, and headache. Emergency medical services found her pulse rate in the 20s. Her initial vital signs in the emergency department were blood pressure of 100/73 mm Hg, heart rate of 49 beats/min, respiratory rate of 27 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation of 95% on a nonrebreather mask.

Patient required intubation for airway protection.

- Imaging Studies:    1. Computed tomography of the head: No acute pathology    2. Chest radiography: Showed pulmonary consolidation    3. Electrocardiogram (ECG):       Image Title: Electrocardiogram During Transcutaneous Pacing       Image Description: ECG showing intrinsic junctional rhythm at rate of about 60 beats/min, and TCP delivering stimuli at about 75 beats/min. Narrow QRS complexes without visible preceding P waves at rate of about 60 beats/min.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Septic shock with anuric kidney failure

clinical_record:
A 33-year-old man with a history of massive small-bowel and ileocecal resection 12 years earlier (leaving 40 cm of small intestine) was maintained on a normal diet after bowel rehabilitation. One month before admission, he developed diarrhea and a 7-kg weight loss with progressive weakness, anorexia, dizziness, and cachexia. On admission his weight was 36 kg (BMI 12.2 kg/m^2), heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 70/50 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 bpm. He was alert and oriented. Physical examination showed pitting edema of the lower extremities, thin skin, a scaphoid abdomen, and no ascites. Chest radiography revealed a dense nodule outside the right upper lung field (thought to be rib calcification). Lower-limb radiographs and renal ultrasonography were normal; gallbladder ultrasonography showed atrophy. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T-wave flattening/inversion in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6, and an incomplete right bundle-branch block. Initial laboratory values included: phosphate 1.10 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.60 mmol/L, calcium 1.7 mmol/L, albumin 27.7 g/L, prealbumin 100 mg/dL, hemoglobin 48 g/L, hematocrit 14.0%, BUN 5.0 mmol/L, and creatinine 86 mg/dL. He was diagnosed with severe malnutrition and received blood transfusion; parenteral nutrition (500 kcal/day); fluids; electrolyte, trace-element, and multivitamin supplementation (including daily thiamine 100 mg IV). Over 24 hours his strength and edema improved. Then he acutely developed profound fatigue and flaccid weakness of all four limbs. His heart rate was 98 bpm, respiratory rate was unchanged, and repeat labs showed a phosphate level of 0.05 mmol/L.

A 70-year-old man with extensive nicotine use and a remote history of laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (7 years prior) and bladder urothelial carcinoma (10 years prior) underwent dual-chamber pacemaker implantation for sick sinus syndrome 9 months ago. Postoperative checks on days 1, 2, and at 3 months showed normal pacemaker function and a clinically unremarkable pocket. Three weeks before presentation, he tested positive for COVID-19 infection, but his fatigue, dyspnea, and cough persisted and worsened rather than improving. At a routine cardiology visit 9 months after implantation, he reported a new, painless but bothersome swelling over the pacemaker site. On examination, his blood pressure and heart rate were normal, and there were no signs of cardiac decompensation or cachexia. Chest ultrasound revealed a soft tissue mass with increased vascularity surrounding the device. CT imaging confirmed a soft-tissue mass around the pacemaker pocket, and haematoma or infection was excluded.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

candidate_registry.label: COVID-19 related pericardial or myocardial inflammation
